fields.expected: I'm an Applied Mathematics & Statistics and Economics undergraduate at Johns Hopkins, and most of my work has been building automation and AI systems that have to survive contact with real workflows. The project closest to this role is a local browser-automation agent I built in TypeScript and Node with Playwright. The problem was repetitive browser work across application systems, but a fully autonomous agent is risky because one wrong action submits something real. I used SQLite as the single source of truth so state cannot diverge across processes, put every application through an explicit state machine, and gated every mutating capability behind fail-closed flags that never default to enabled. Free-text and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from auto-filling and always generate a human-review item. At Intelehealth I designed an evaluation framework comparing LLM-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard, which taught me that generating an answer is cheap and deciding whether to trust it is the hard part. That's the mindset I'd bring to AI and automation work at a firm where accuracy and review matter: figure out where automation should stop, not only where it can go. I'd like to own real pieces of a system and learn from people who use it daily.

fields.expected:
Another piece of my background that fits an AI and automation role is the evaluation work I did at Intelehealth. I designed an evaluation framework for AI-generated clinical outputs against a benchmark of 4,169 cases, using stratified sampling to compare model outputs to a clinical standard and surface systematic failure modes. That work changed how I think about AI systems: generating an answer with an LLM is cheap, but deciding whether it should be trusted is the harder problem, and in a firm setting that judgment is the whole ballgame.

I currently build the machine-learning core of an anomaly-detection and alert-prioritization system at Summer Atlantic Capital, including the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI detection service, temporal sequence models over event streams, a learning-to-rank layer for alerts, and a retrieval-augmented explanation layer so analysts can see why something was flagged. The constraint I care most about there is operational usefulness: a system that floods people with alerts creates a second problem instead of solving the first.

fields.expected:
A third piece I'd point to is the anomaly-detection and alert-prioritization system I'm building at Summer Atlantic Capital / SAC Nexus. I own major parts of the data and ML infrastructure: the repository and CI scaffold, the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, and the public detection API. The modeling side uses temporal sequence models over event streams with RNN and Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, and a learning-to-rank layer that decides which alerts a human should look at first. I also built an LLM explanation layer with retrieval-augmented generation so the output arrives as something an analyst can read and act on rather than a bare score.

What I've learned there is that model performance is not the hard part. An anomaly system that fires too often just creates a second problem, so prioritization, explanation quality, known failure modes, and documentation matter as much as the detector itself. That's the mindset I'd bring to internal automation work at Bennett Thrasher: build something people in the firm will actually keep using, and be honest about where it should stop and hand off to a person.

fields.expected: A fourth project I'd point to is tSearch, a talent-discovery system I built in TypeScript and Node with Playwright, Express, and OpenAI. It starts from named seed candidates, expands through public collaboration and publishing graphs like GitHub and Substack, and runs a pipeline of identity resolution, graph expansion, heuristic scoring, persistence, LLM assessment, and a recruiter digest. Two design decisions mattered most. First, missing evidence is never treated as negative evidence: if the system can't find enough public work to judge a dimension, it returns "insufficient evidence" rather than a low score. Second, discovery and assessment stay separate, so the LLM judges can't silently paper over an identity-resolution mistake or collapse the heuristic score into their own. The judging layer is rubric-driven, with parallel judges on separate dimensions synthesized into an evidence-cited assessment. It's the same instinct I'd bring to internal automation work: build the pipeline, then make its failure modes visible instead of hidden.
